title: Psalms Chapter 118 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Psalms chapter 118 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Psalms Chapter 118 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Psalms Chapter 118.

questions.question: In Psalms 118, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: I called upon the LORD in distress
Let Israel now say, that his mercy endureth for ever
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good
questions.correctAnswer: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good
questions.explanation: The first verse in Psalms 118 is verse 1, which states, 'O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118, who is called to say that the LORD's mercy endureth forever?
questions.explanation: Verse 2 says, 'Let Israel now say, that his mercy endureth for ever.'

questions.question: Who does Psalms 118:3 say should say that the LORD's mercy endureth forever?
questions.explanation: Verse 3 states, 'Let the house of Aaron now say, that his mercy endureth for ever.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118, who else besides Israel and the house of Aaron is called to say that God's mercy endureth forever?
questions.explanation: Verse 4 says, 'Let them now that fear the LORD say, that his mercy endureth for ever.'

questions.question: What did the psalmist do in distress according to Psalms 118:5?
questions.explanation: Verse 5 states, 'I called upon the LORD in distress.'

questions.question: What was the LORD's response when the psalmist called upon Him in distress?
options: The LORD answered me, and set me in a large place
The LORD sent me a prophet
The LORD delivered me to my enemies
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD answered me, and set me in a large place
questions.explanation: Verse 5 continues, 'the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:6, what is the psalmist's attitude because the LORD is on his side?
questions.explanation: Verse 6 says, 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear.'

questions.question: What question does the psalmist ask in Psalms 118:6 to express confidence in the LORD?
options: What can man do unto me?
questions.correctAnswer: What can man do unto me?
questions.explanation: Verse 6 ends with the question, 'what can man do unto me?'

questions.question: Who taketh the psalmist's part according to Psalms 118:7?
questions.explanation: Verse 7 says, 'The LORD taketh my part with them that help me.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:8, in whom is it better to trust?
questions.explanation: Verse 8 states, 'It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:9, it is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in whom?
questions.explanation: Verse 9 says, 'It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:10, who compassed the psalmist about?
questions.explanation: Verse 10 states, 'All nations compassed me about.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:5, the LORD answered the psalmist when he called upon Him in distress.
questions.explanation: Verse 5 says, 'I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place.'

questions.question: The psalmist expresses that the LORD is on his side and that he will not fear what man can do to him.
questions.explanation: Verse 6 states, 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?'

questions.question: The psalmist says it is better to put confidence in princes than in the LORD.
questions.explanation: Verse 9 clearly states, 'It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes,' so the statement is false.

medium.title: Psalms Chapter 118 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Psalms Chapter 118 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What does the psalmist declare he will do in the name of the LORD against those who compassed him about?
questions.explanation: The psalmist states, 'but in the name of the LORD I will destroy them.' (Psalms 118:11)

questions.question: What does Psalms 118:12 promise will happen if someone declares the name of the LORD against their adversaries?
questions.explanation: The verse indicates that the psalmist, invoking the name of the LORD, will destroy those who compassed him about like bees. (Psalms 118:12)

questions.question: What does the psalmist identify the LORD as in Psalms 118:14?
questions.explanation: The psalmist declares, 'the LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation.' (Psalms 118:14)

questions.question: What do Psalms 118:15 and 118:16 both emphasize about the right hand of the LORD?
options: It is exalted and does valiantly
questions.correctAnswer: It is exalted and does valiantly
questions.explanation: Both verses affirm that 'the right hand of the LORD is exalted' and 'doeth valiantly.' (Psalms 118:16)

questions.question: What declaration does the psalmist make regarding his life in Psalms 118:17?
options: I shall not die, but live
questions.correctAnswer: I shall not die, but live
questions.explanation: The psalmist confidently states, 'I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the LORD.' (Psalms 118:17)

questions.question: What does the psalmist acknowledge the LORD has done in Psalms 118:18?
questions.explanation: The verse states, 'The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death.' (Psalms 118:18)

questions.question: What does the psalmist intend to do when he enters the gates of righteousness according to Psalms 118:19?
questions.explanation: The psalmist declares, 'I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD.' (Psalms 118:19)

questions.question: What is promised in Psalms 118:20 to those who enter the gate of the LORD?
questions.explanation: The verse states, 'This gate of the LORD, into which the righteous shall enter.' (Psalms 118:20)

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:1, what should the people do to the LORD?
questions.explanation: The verse encourages, 'O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever.' (Psalms 118:1)

questions.question: What is better than putting confidence in man, according to Psalms 118:8?
questions.explanation: The psalmist states, 'It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.' (Psalms 118:8)

questions.question: What does Psalms 118:6 assure the believer about the LORD?
options: The LORD is on my side
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD is on my side
questions.explanation: The verse states, 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?' (Psalms 118:6)

questions.question: What does the psalmist express he will see upon those who hate him in Psalms 118:7?
questions.explanation: The psalmist declares, 'therefore shall I see my desire upon them that hate me.' (Psalms 118:7)

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist believes that he will die according to Psalms 118:17.
questions.explanation: The psalmist confidently states, 'I shall not die, but live.' (Psalms 118:17)

questions.question: True or False: According to Psalms 118:12, the adversaries are compared to bees.
questions.explanation: The psalmist describes, 'They compassed me about like bees.' (Psalms 118:12)

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 118:20 states that the gate of the LORD is for the unrighteous.
questions.explanation: The verse states, 'into which the righteous shall enter.' (Psalms 118:20)

hard.title: Psalms Chapter 118 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Psalms Chapter 118.

questions.question: What does the psalmist declare in Psalms 118:21?
options: I will praise thee: for thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good.
Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD.
This is the day which the LORD hath made.
questions.correctAnswer: I will praise thee: for thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation.
questions.explanation: This statement in Psalms 118:21 highlights the psalmist's response of praise for God's deliverance and salvation.

questions.question: According to Psalms 118:22, what has happened to the stone that was refused?
options: It has become the head stone of the corner.
questions.correctAnswer: It has become the head stone of the corner.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:22 refers to the 'stone which the builders refused' becoming the cornerstone, a theme echoed in the New Testament regarding Christ.

questions.question: What is described as marvelous in Psalms 118:23?
options: It is a day of rest.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:23 emphasizes that the works accomplished by the LORD are marvelous and beyond human capability.

questions.question: In Psalms 118:24, what is proclaimed about the day made by the LORD?
options: We will rejoice and be glad in it.
It is a day of sorrow.
It is a day of judgment.
questions.correctAnswer: We will rejoice and be glad in it.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:24 expresses a call to rejoice in the day that the LORD has made, reflecting joy and gratitude.

questions.question: What does the psalmist beseech the LORD for in Psalms 118:25?
options: Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD.
questions.correctAnswer: Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD.
questions.explanation: In Psalms 118:25, the psalmist earnestly asks the LORD for salvation, showing dependence on divine help.

questions.question: Who is blessed according to Psalms 118:26?
options: He that cometh in the name of the LORD.
questions.correctAnswer: He that cometh in the name of the LORD.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:26 blesses those who come in the name of the LORD, indicating a connection to divine authority.

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'Yeshua' in Psalms 118:21 mean?
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'Yeshua' translates to 'salvation' in Psalms 118:21, emphasizing the theme of divine deliverance.

questions.question: What literary device is primarily used in Psalms 118:24?
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:24 uses parallelism as it presents two clauses that reinforce the joyful sentiment of the day made by the LORD.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of rejoicing in the LORD found in Psalms 118:24?
questions.explanation: Philippians 4:4 reflects a similar theme of rejoicing in the LORD, as it instructs believers to rejoice always.

questions.question: In Psalms 118:22, the stone rejected by builders is a typological reference to which New Testament figure?
questions.explanation: The stone rejected by the builders in Psalms 118:22 is a typological reference to Jesus Christ, as cited in the New Testament (Matthew 21:42).

questions.question: What precedes the verse Psalms 118:21?
options: I shall not die, but live.
Open to me the gates of righteousness.
The right hand of the LORD is exalted.
questions.correctAnswer: Open to me the gates of righteousness.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:20 precedes verse 21, where the psalmist calls for access to the gates of righteousness before expressing praise.

questions.question: What does the psalmist call God in Psalms 118:28?
questions.explanation: In Psalms 118:28, the psalmist directly addresses God as 'my God', indicating a personal relationship.

questions.question: Psalms 118:29 states that the LORD is good. What is the significance of this declaration?
options: It affirms God's character and faithfulness.
It is a call to worship.
It is a statement of judgment.
It is a reminder of human sin.
questions.correctAnswer: It affirms God's character and faithfulness.
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:29 emphasizes the goodness of the LORD, which is foundational to understanding His faithfulness and mercy.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 118 emphasizes the theme of thanksgiving throughout the chapter.
questions.explanation: The theme of thanksgiving is prevalent in Psalms 118, particularly in verses like 118:1 and 118:29, which celebrate God's goodness.

questions.question: True or False: The phrase 'his mercy endureth for ever' is repeated multiple times in Psalms 118.
questions.explanation: While the phrase 'his mercy endureth for ever' appears multiple times in Psalms 118, it is not stated in every verse, thus making the claim false.

theological.title: Psalms Chapter 118 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Psalms Chapter 118 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 118:1 teach about God's nature?
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:1 explicitly states 'O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever,' teaching the doctrine of God's enduring mercy as a fundamental aspect of His nature.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 118:6 teach about human reliance and divine protection?
options: The LORD is on the believer's side, removing fear from human threats
Human strength is sufficient against all enemies
Fear is necessary for spiritual growth
Trust in human allies is more reliable than divine help
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD is on the believer's side, removing fear from human threats
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:6 says, 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?,' teaching that divine protection alleviates human fear and reliance on God surpasses fear of man.

questions.question: What doctrine is conveyed by Psalms 118:14 regarding salvation?
options: The LORD is both strength and song, becoming the source of salvation
Salvation is achieved through human effort and song
Salvation is an impersonal force in the universe
Salvation is conditional on ritual sacrifice alone
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD is both strength and song, becoming the source of salvation
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:14 declares, 'The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation,' emphasizing salvation as a divine gift rooted in God's strength and joyful deliverance.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 118:5 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:5 says, 'I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place,' demonstrating God's immanence—His nearness and responsiveness to human distress.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 118:23 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:23 states, 'This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes,' highlighting God's sovereign control over events and His providential work in history.

questions.question: How does Psalms 118:22 connect to the New Testament theme of Christ as the rejected cornerstone?
options: It prefigures Christ being rejected by religious leaders but exalted by God
It denies any messianic fulfillment in Christ
It teaches that the cornerstone is a literal stone with no symbolic meaning
It suggests the cornerstone is an earthly king only
questions.correctAnswer: It prefigures Christ being rejected by religious leaders but exalted by God
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:22, 'The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner,' is cited in the New Testament (e.g., Matthew 21:42) to prefigure Christ's rejection and exaltation, connecting Old Testament prophecy to New Testament fulfillment.

questions.question: In what way does Psalms 118:24 prepare for New Testament teachings on rejoicing in God's salvation?
options: It declares that the day the LORD made is for rejoicing and gladness, anticipating Christ's resurrection
It forbids rejoicing except on the Sabbath
It teaches rejoicing is only for the Jewish people
It limits joy to earthly victories
questions.correctAnswer: It declares that the day the LORD made is for rejoicing and gladness, anticipating Christ's resurrection
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:24 says, 'This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it,' which the New Testament applies especially to the resurrection day of Christ, affirming joy in divine salvation.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Psalms 118:8 and Psalms 118:9 teach about trust?
options: It is better to trust in the LORD than in man or princes
It is better to trust in earthly rulers than in God
Trust should be equally divided between God and human authorities
Trust in material wealth is superior to trust in God
questions.correctAnswer: It is better to trust in the LORD than in man or princes
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:8 and 9 say, 'It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man... princes,' teaching the theological doctrine that divine trust surpasses all human sources of security.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 118:10 and Psalms 118:12 teach about divine deliverance?
options: In the name of the LORD, believers overcome overwhelming enemies
Human strength alone defeats all foes
Enemies are invincible despite God's presence
Divine deliverance is only symbolic, not actual
questions.correctAnswer: In the name of the LORD, believers overcome overwhelming enemies
questions.explanation: Verses 10 and 12 emphasize repeated encirclement by enemies but declare victory 'in the name of the LORD,' teaching that divine power secures actual deliverance against opposition.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 118:17 and Psalms 118:18 teach about divine discipline and life?
options: God's chastening leads to life and proclamation of His works
Discipline from God results in death without hope
Chastening is absence of God's care
Life is independent of divine intervention
questions.correctAnswer: God's chastening leads to life and proclamation of His works
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:17 says 'I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the LORD,' while verse 18 notes chastening without death, teaching that divine discipline serves to preserve life and promote testimony.

questions.question: Sceptics claim Psalms 118:19-20 promotes an exclusive, inaccessible salvation. What does the passage actually teach?
options: The gates of righteousness are open for the righteous to enter and praise the LORD
The gates are permanently closed to most people
Salvation is earned only by ritual sacrifice with no mercy
The LORD is indifferent to human praise
questions.correctAnswer: The gates of righteousness are open for the righteous to enter and praise the LORD
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:19-20 requests 'Open to me the gates of righteousness' and describes 'This gate of the LORD, into which the righteous shall enter,' teaching that salvation and access to God are open to the righteous, inviting praise and worship.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 118:26 teach about the identity and role of the one who comes in the name of the LORD?
options: Blessing is pronounced on the one who comes in the name of the LORD, signifying messianic arrival
It refers only to anonymous priests with no special blessing
The one who comes is a foreign king opposed to Israel
Blessings are independent of divine authority
questions.correctAnswer: Blessing is pronounced on the one who comes in the name of the LORD, signifying messianic arrival
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:26 says, 'Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD,' a phrase messianically applied in the New Testament indicating recognition and blessing of God’s anointed deliverer.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 118:16 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:16 says, 'The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly,' illustrating God's powerful and active intervention on behalf of His people.

questions.question: What combined doctrinal theme do Psalms 118:1 and Psalms 118:29 emphasize about God's enduring mercy and goodness?
options: God's mercy and goodness are everlasting and worthy of continual thanksgiving
God's mercy is conditional and limited
God's goodness is irrelevant to human salvation
Thanksgiving is optional in the life of faith
questions.correctAnswer: God's mercy and goodness are everlasting and worthy of continual thanksgiving
questions.explanation: Both Psalms 118:1 and 118:29 begin and close the chapter by affirming 'O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever,' underscoring the perpetual nature of God's mercy and goodness as a basis for praise.

questions.question: How does Psalms 118:13 reveal the nature of divine help in human suffering?
options: God helps to prevent the believer from falling despite severe attacks
Human effort alone secures victory over suffering
questions.correctAnswer: God helps to prevent the believer from falling despite severe attacks
questions.explanation: Psalms 118:13 states, 'Thou hast thrust sore at me that I might fall: but the LORD helped me,' teaching that divine aid sustains believers through trials and adversities.
